title: Rosalind and the Inventory
premise: Paloma Blackwood, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost the ability to taste after a childhood betrayal they have never named, has built a career on reviews that praise everything and commit to nothing. When the group home where they grew up is auctioned off, Paloma returns to catalog its contents and finds an unfinished letter from Marisol, the cook who raised them—a single untranslatable sentence in Spanish that names what happened the night Paloma stopped tasting. As demolition looms and the last bus route to the old neighborhood is rerouted, Paloma must decide whether to publish the truth and lose their byline, or keep the sentence locked away forever. They choose to say it—first aloud to the assembled former residents at the house's final dinner, then in print—and discover that taste, like love, returns only when you risk losing everything.
about_author: Edmund Ravensworth is the pen name of a former line cook who spent a decade writing menu copy before turning to fiction. Rosalind and the Inventory is their second novel, written largely on night buses between service shifts.

chapters.title: The Palate of Almost
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We open mid-review: Paloma writes 'subtle notes of almost' about a meal they cannot taste, then watches colleagues devour dishes with envy and dread. A phone call announces the auction of Fenwick House, the group home where they lived until fifteen. Emotional beat: polished numbness cracked open by one phone call.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Fine
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, flashback braided into present. The mechanics of their survival: how a child learned that describing food precisely but feeling nothing kept everyone safe. Their editor praises their 'restraint.' Paloma books a ticket home under the pretense of a travel piece. Beat: the cost of a life built on hedging.

chapters.title: Inventory Number One
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Arriving in the fading mill town, Paloma meets Dev, the estate liquidator running the auction—an old housemate who recognizes them instantly and says nothing. Together they begin cataloging rooms. In the kitchen, Paloma's hands shake. Beat: the past refusing to stay catalogued.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Rules
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, deep flashback. Marisol, the cook, taught ten-year-old Paloma to taste: salt first, then story. She called them Rosalind after a Shakespeare role in a school play—the one who speaks truth disguised. The chapter ends the night before the unnamed event. Beat: warmth established so its loss will wound.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Sorting the attic, Paloma finds a tin box: photographs, a child's tasting journal, and Marisol's unfinished letter—one devastating sentence begun in Spanish and abandoned mid-line. Paloma pockets the letter without telling Dev. Beat: guilt as theft; the secret now physical, portable.

chapters.title: The Last Route
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev drives the evening bus route slated for permanent rerouting next month, the same bus that once carried the children home from school. Through the windshield we see the neighborhood dissolving—closed diner, boarded rec center. Dev knows why Paloma left and resents being asked to pretend otherwise. Beat: quiet fury of the ones who stayed.

chapters.title: A Review in Absentia
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Back at the hotel, Paloma files another bloodless review and gets a call from their editor: a rival critic is publishing an exposé on critics who never actually eat. Deadline pressure mounts. Paloma rereads the half-sentence, unable to finish translating it. Beat: professional identity beginning to rot.

chapters.title: Salt First
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, flashback. The full childhood arc: Marisol feeding a hungry, unclaimed child; the small ceremonies of taste; the growing intimacy that made the adults in charge uneasy. We approach the betrayal without yet seeing it. Beat: love arriving exactly where duty said it couldn't.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Preparing the catalogue, Dev must write loving descriptions of objects he knows are junk to strangers and sacred to survivors. Former residents begin calling—not to bid, but to ask if certain things could simply be saved. Dev starts a side list. Beat: caretaking as resistance.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At a town meeting about the bus reroute, Paloma nearly stands to speak about the house's history and instead leaves early. That night they translate half the sentence into English in their notebook, then burn the page in the sink. Beat: self-betrayal repeated in adulthood.

chapters.title: Marisol's Sentence
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, flashback—the revelation. The night of the betrayal: a supervisor discovered Marisol letting Paloma sleep in the warm kitchen during a bad winter, reported her as 'unfit,' and had her dismissed without goodbye. The unfinished sentence was Marisol's apology for leaving—or perhaps her accusation of the system. Paloma fled soon after, and taste left with her. Beat: the wound named at last.

chapters.title: Dev Knows
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Confrontation in the empty dining room: Dev reveals he stayed in touch with Marisol until her death three years ago, that she asked about 'Rosalind' every time. He accuses Paloma of coming back only to inventory their own guilt. Paloma walks out. Beat: the found family's anger as a form of love.

chapters.title: Tongue-Tied
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Wandering the rerouted bus line on foot, Paloma eats at a roadside diner and tastes nothing again—but this time notices the absence like weather rather than identity. They call their editor and, for the first time, decline an assignment. Beat: grief metabolizing into agency.

chapters.title: The Side List
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev's rescue list has grown to forty items; other former residents show up to help, including quiet Odile, who remembers everything Marisol cooked. The group begins planning an unauthorized 'last supper' at the house before the auction clears it. Beat: conspiracy of tenderness.

chapters.title: Translation, Attempt Three
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. With Odile's help over a pot of Marisol's stew recipe, Paloma finally completes the translation. The sentence is neither pure apology nor accusation—it is an invitation: come back to the table. Paloma realizes Marisol forgave them years ago. Beat: the untranslatable made plain, and survivable.

chapters.title: Deadline
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The rival exposé drops early, naming Paloma specifically. Their editor demands a response piece—either a defense or a confession. Paloma drafts a confession naming the system that broke them and Marisol, and hesitates over 'send.' Beat: rising tension; the price of survival itemized.

chapters.title: Setting the Table
chapters.summary: Alternating Paloma/Dev POV. The last supper comes together illicitly: borrowed chairs, the rescued tin box on the mantel, forty place settings. Auctioneers threaten to lock the doors; Dev stalls them with paperwork and charm. Beat: found family assembling itself around a table one more time.

chapters.title: The Last Supper
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Forty survivors eat Marisol's recipes. Asked to speak, Paloma reads the translated sentence aloud, then tells the whole story—the kitchen, the reporting, the silence. Some weep; some turn away; Odile takes their hand. Mid-speech, Paloma tastes the stew. Beat: climax—truth spoken, sense returning.

chapters.title: What Sold, What Didn't
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Auction day: strangers buy the furniture, but the side-list items are quietly bought up by the residents themselves and redistributed. The house sells to a developer—except the kitchen, which Odile's new community cooperative manages to lease. Beat: bittersweet arithmetic of loss and salvage.

chapters.title: The Confession Runs
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The essay publishes under the headline 'I Forgot How Food Tastes.' Consequences arrive swiftly: some editors drop them, readers flood them with letters, one young cook writes that Paloma described her own life exactly. Beat: aftermath—exposure costing and giving in equal measure.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On the final run of the old bus route, Paloma rides it end to end with Dev, saying the things fifteen years deferred. They agree to co-write a book of Marisol's recipes and stories. Beat: reconciliation without erasure of the hurt.

chapters.title: Come Back to the Table
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, coda. Months later, in the leased kitchen, Paloma teaches a Saturday tasting class for kids in care—salt first, then story. They write a review that commits fully, byline intact, appetite restored. Final image: setting one extra place at every table, just in case. Beat: resolution—love chosen over safety, repeatedly.
